core_obligations: Reduce to nonempty equidimensional schemes (proof lines 2935-2952): the empty cases follow from the vanishing of the cohomology of the empty scheme; separately, the two schemes can be replaced by products with projective spaces so that they are equidimensional of the same dimension and admit morphisms to the originals with sections, which makes the pullback injective and preserves the injectivity question.

Injectivity through idempotents (proof lines 2952-2973): the class of the disjoint union is the sum of the classes of the two components, which are orthogonal idempotents by the unit and pushforward lemmas and the behaviour of the cycle class map on zero cycles; the projection formula then exhibits any class as the sum of the pullbacks of its restrictions, giving injectivity.

Surjectivity (proof lines 2973-3007): the classes of the components pull back to one and zero on the respective summands by axiom (C), so surjectivity of the comparison map follows from surjectivity of the restriction to one component; that restriction is surjective as soon as there is a morphism from the other component to it, and such a morphism exists after base changing along a finite separable extension over which a rational closed point exists; axiom (B) and nonvanishing of cohomology reduce the statement to that case.
proof_roadmap: Handle the empty cases and reduce to nonempty equidimensional schemes of the same dimension.
Use the orthogonal idempotents given by the classes of the components for injectivity.
Reduce surjectivity to the existence of a morphism, obtained after a finite separable base change.
difficulty_reason: The lemma proves that the cohomology of a disjoint union of two smooth projective schemes is the product of the cohomologies, for a theory satisfying the data and axioms (A), (B), (C) (statement lines 2931-2940). The proof (proof lines 2941-3007) handles the empty cases, reduces to equidimensional schemes of the same dimension, uses orthogonal idempotents for injectivity, and obtains surjectivity after a finite separable base change providing a rational point. H3: an injectivity and surjectivity argument with a base change reduction, written out in full.
